newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia disappointed by US NATO enlargement stance.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia disappointed by US NATO enlargement stance.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek conceded on Friday the country's chances of joining NATO before 2000 had diminished but held out the hope of a last-minute change of heart in Washington.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Thursday NATO's eastward expansion should include the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary. He left out Slovenia and Romania.
"Yesterday's message from the U.S. took us by surprise, and not in a positive way," Drnovsek told a news conference.
"Our chances for inclusion are very small but they still exist. Some NATO members said a last minute compromise was possible," he added.

The prime minister vowed to press on with efforts to gain support from European members of the alliance, Canada and the U.S. Congress. Italy has already reinforced its support for Slovenia and Romania, arguing their inclusion would maintain a balance between NATO's northern and southern flanks.
NATO members will reach their final decision on new members at a Madrid summit on July 8 and 9.

"If Slovenia is not included it will not be a tragedy as we are not threatened by anyone at the moment. But for our long-term interests we believe it would be better for Slovenia to be included in NATO," Drnovsek said.

He rejected speculation that the U.S. stance on NATO would hamper Slovenia in its bid to join the European Union in the first round of its eastward enlargement. The prime minister said he had already received a assurances in a telephone conversation with European Commission President Jacques Santer.
"In world politics there are compensations. Therefore support for Slovenia's candidacy to join the EU is likely to increase as a compensation (for the NATO decision)," he said.
Slovenia, the richest and northernmost of the former Yugoslav republics, has placed enormous emphasis on being included in western organisations since it broke away from Belgrade in 1991.

Last week the government announced plans to amend the constitution in order to bring property laws into line with European norms and remove the last remaining obstacles to EU membership. At present foreigners are not permitted to own real estate in Slovenia.
"If we change the 68th article of our constitution in late June or early July than our candidacy to join the EU in the first round will not be questioned," Drnovsek said.
"That was confirmed by the European Commission President Jacques Santer in our telephone discussion today," he continued.
Drnovsek said he planned no government changes if the country failed to win NATO membership.
"I am sure we did everything we could. We gained strong support among most NATO member states and in the U.S. Congress and improved Slovenia's international position," he said.
